expected_evidence: Elevated cosmogenic/nucleogenic radionuclide spikes (10Be, 36Cl, 14C) in Greenland ice cores (GISP2/GRIP/NEEM) synchronous with the Younger Dryas onset, consistent with a burst of ionizing radiation rather than solar-modulated production
Anomalous concentration of nitrate (NO3-) or other odd-nitrogen species in the same ice layers, as gamma/cosmic-ray ionization of the atmosphere is expected to boost NOx production
Isotopic signatures specific to nucleosynthesis (e.g., 60Fe or other supernova-tracer isotopes) in ice or deep-sea sediment layers dated to ~12,900 years BP

Identification of a supernova remnant (via proper-motion/expansion-age dating of a known SNR, or a pulsar with a characteristic age) located close enough and correctly aged (~13,000 yr) to have irradiated Earth
Ozone-depletion proxies or a UV-flux signature in contemporaneous sediment/ice biomarkers, since gamma-ray-induced ozone loss is a predicted secondary effect
Corroborating abrupt climate-proxy shift (dust, methane, oxygen isotopes) at the exact same ice-core depth/date as the radionuclide anomaly
Possible oral-tradition motifs of a 'sky fire' or sudden darkness event, though at 13,000 years remove this is a weak/speculative category
Absence-of-alternative-cause argument: ruling out solar proton events, geomagnetic excursions, or cometary/impact debris (e.g., platinum, microspherules) as the source of any detected anomaly
response.rationale: The hypothesis is testable primarily through two high-detectability channels for this period: astronomical (0.7) and geological/ice-core (0.65) evidence — both because Greenland ice sheets preserve continuous, datable radionuclide and chemistry records spanning the Younger Dryas onset, and because a sufficiently close/young supernova remnant would leave an identifiable astrophysical trace (expansion age, remnant morphology, or isotopic ejecta) that survives for millennia. These are the channels this hypothesis is actually built on (mechanism='gamma-ray-ionization', place='greenland-ice-sheet'), so if the event occurred, its two strongest fingerprints (isotope spike + candidate SNR) are exactly the kinds of evidence with decent survival odds. However, corroborating evidence from material (0.35), genetic (0.3), oral_tradition (0.1), iconographic (0.1), and textual (0.0) channels is essentially unavailable for an Upper Paleolithic/Younger Dryas-era population with no writing and only fragile transmission of oral narratives across 13,000 years — so total absence of evidence there is expected and uninformative about truth. Existing ice-core studies (GISP2/GRIP/NEEM) have in fact been searched for anomalous 10Be/36Cl/nitrate spikes at the YD boundary; results are debated and no unambiguous gamma-ray/supernova signature (as opposed to competing solar-event or comet-impact explanations) has been robustly confirmed, and no supernova remnant of the required age/proximity has been securely identified — this is consistent with either the hypothesis being false or the specific isotopic/astrophysical signal being weak, ambiguous, or already eroded/overprinted by 13 millennia of ice flow and diagenesis. Given the strong reliance on the two well-preserved channels but the real possibility of signal ambiguity and lack of a confirmed source remnant, a moderate overall detectability_adjustment (~0.55, below the naive 0.7/0.65 astronomical/geological figures but well above the near-zero textual/oral channels) is warranted; this treats the current absence of a clearly corroborated signal as only weak evidence against the hypothesis rather than a decisive falsification, since much of the required corroboration (a specific matching SNR, unambiguous isotope attribution) is inherently hard to detect even if the event were real (model-prior: the supernova/gamma-ray YD-trigger idea is a real but minority proposal in the literature, distinct from and less supported than the mainstream comet-impact YDB hypothesis).
